YouTuber Builds Stealth Shield That Blinds Police Flock Surveillance Cameras

TB
By Tyler Brooks Viral Concepts & Prototype Lead • via Jalopnik Wire
⚡ Visual Story
Source & Photography: Jalopnik Wire Dispatch Verified Editorial Asset
⚡ Executive Takeaways & Key Highlights
  • Flock cameras take an unimaginably huge number of pictures of cars and license plates, creating a searchable database of times and locations that can be used to track your movements.
  • If you don't care to participate, you can use apps like MapQuest to avoid these cameras , or FlockHopper to automatically route around them.
  • Official reporting verified via Jalopnik news desk.
⚡ EDITORIAL TAKE • TYLER BROOKS Viral Concepts & Prototype Lead

Automotive Innovation & Market Feasibility

Concept prototypes and viral vehicle reveals offer an exciting window into the automotive industry's future design language. Dispatches from Jalopnik demonstrate how radical styling, lightweight materials, and powertrain packaging can transition from design studios to production assembly lines. Engineering feasibility and homologation standards remain the true measures of impact.

Big Picture: Market reception and formal OEM production announcements will determine which concept innovations make it to consumer streets.

Flock cameras take an unimaginably huge number of pictures of cars and license plates, creating a searchable database of times and locations that can be used to track your movements. If you don't care to participate, you can use apps like MapQuest to avoid these cameras , or FlockHopper to automatically route around them. Or you can do as YouTuber Studio Hotrods did, and design a system to make your license plate invisible, but only near a Flock camera.

📌 The Core Development

What Studio Hotrods came up with is a clever system that obscures your plate only when you're in view of a Flock camera. The video goes into detail, but basically, an Arduino computer controls a piece of smart glass that's clear when it receives power but turns opaque when the power shuts off. This smart glass goes over the license plate.

The Arduino is also connected to a GPS antenna and module that tells it the vehicle's location, which it cross-references with an SD card containing a database of Flock camera locations, likely by the DeFlock mapping project . Under normal driving conditions, the smart glass receives power and remains clear, keeping the license plate visible as is legally required. When the vehicle passes a Flock camera, however, it briefly turns the smart glass opaque, just long enough to prevent the camera from scanning the plate.

🔍 Background & Sector Context

This seems like a pretty neat idea. Unless a cop is looking right at your license plate at the moment you pass a Flock camera, they're still going to see your plate, so there shouldn't be a problem, right? Unfortunately, it's not as simple as that.

According to Allowed Here , every state has some kind of restriction on license plate covers. They are illegal in eight states, including Illinois, where the car used for testing in this video is registered. States that haven't banned covers outright still require the plate to be legible, and they may not obscure the plate in any way. Depending on where you live, you could still get pulled over just for having a cover on your license plate, even if it's as clear as glass at the time.

📊 Industry & Real-World Impact

States are already cracking down on license plate flippers , which obscure plates both from cops and automatic toll cameras. Studio Hotrods' "Flock-O-Matic" system recognizes these valid reasons, which is why it keeps the plate visible unless you're in direct view of a Flock camera. But the law doesn't care what your intentions are, only that the plate can't be obscured. Plus, it's easy to skip the Arduino and turn the smart glass clear and opaque manually, blocking your plate anytime you want. Cops don't generally like that.

🔮 Strategic Outlook & What Lies Ahead

While Studio Hotrods is designing, testing, and even working on a patent for this device, it's not selling it at this time. A hobbyist with some programming skill could probably figure out how to make something similar — for testing purposes only, of course. In many places, using it on the street is likely to get you the very attention you're trying to avoid.
